analysis.title: Global Energy Weekly: Oil turns blue
key_insights: Global oil supply disruptions reached a record in 2026, larger than anything in the data back to 1965. BofA estimates about 18mn b/d of supply was offline at the peak, and the IEA estimated more than 10mn b/d of Gulf production was shut in during August.

The market entered the conflict well supplied after several quarters of surplus. Global stocks BofA tracks weekly peaked at 6.0bn barrels in March and are being drawn down fast, with floating storage disappearing quickly. The IEA estimated observed global inventories fell by 507mn barrels between February and August.

Global inventories fell at about 2.8mn b/d per IEA figures, while BofA believes demand destruction exceeded 3mn b/d for much of the conflict. Chinese commercial stocks are at very low seasonally adjusted levels and BofA believes China has started tapping its strategic reserves.
China crude imports peaked near 13mn b/d in December 2025 and fell to a low of 7.5mn b/d in June before rebounding somewhat. Conservation has cut apparent demand across many categories.

OECD stocks fell from 1.2bn to 1.0bn barrels from January to the latest reading, about 1mn b/d. The IEA notes OECD stocks rose in August as commercial builds more than offset a 19mn barrel draw in government stocks. Lower strategic stocks leave OECD economies exposed to another shock.

The Brent curve is back in steep backwardation. The front-over-third-month Brent premium peaked at $21/bbl, a very rare level. Dated Brent has traded at a steep premium to front-month futures, which points to acute prompt physical scarcity.

Long-dated crude prices have barely moved during the US-Iran conflict, and WCS at Hardisty has not rallied much past marginal cost of production. The forward curve still discounts a significant normalization of supply over 2 to 3 years. Prediction markets see no near-term resolution but put more weight on a deal within 12-24 months.

Middle East crude exports through Hormuz have recovered and likely averaged 7.4mn b/d in September, but shipping incidents picked up in October. Middle East product exports have not recovered, so refined products are tighter than crude.

Chinese product exports to the rest of Asia have risen over the past 5 months, which depresses Asia Pacific fuel markets relative to the Atlantic Basin, where the shortage is acute. Shanghai crude has at times priced above Atlantic Brent contracts.
Shipping costs from the Persian Gulf to Asia have at times exceeded $60/bbl in total unit cost. Wet-freight rates have surged, longer routes have raised oil on water, and insurance rates are higher.

Russian product exports fell from 2.4mn b/d in 2025 to 1.1mn b/d in July after repeated Ukrainian strikes on refineries. Global refinery utilization is low, and the IEA put August throughput at 81.4mn b/d, 4.2mn b/d lower YoY.
ICE gasoil cracks and global gasoline cracks remain exceptionally high even after the summer driving season ended. Atlantic Basin refining margins hit a record in August, led by diesel.

Demand has held up. The global composite PMI is 55, US oil demand is holding, and BofA economists forecast 3.4% global real GDP growth for 2026, down only 0.1% from the start of the year. Energy spending relative to GDP and US disposable income remains below levels associated with energy-driven recessions.

BofA attributes the economy's resilience to inventory use, lax fiscal and monetary policy, and the AI investment cycle. The US is a large net energy exporter with a deficit near 6% of GDP, and BofA estimates the net impact of the war on US GDP has so far been positive.

US market share of global oil and gas is at a record while OPEC's share has collapsed. A full normalization needs geopolitical stability and restored production and shipping routes. Saudi Arabia has rerouted nearly 4mn b/d through the East-West pipeline, supporting Suez crossings.

BofA keeps Brent forecasts at $96 for 2H26 and $80 for 2027. A ceasefire could push Brent toward $80 or lower on average in 2027. A 'neither war nor peace' scenario could hold Brent around triple digits. Renewed US-Iran conflict could push Brent toward $150/bbl in 2027.

sector_views.rationale: Physical markets are very tight with depleted inventories, steep backwardation and record refining margins. BofA still expects Brent to fall to $80 in 2027 if the conflicts ease.

macro_indicators.interpretation: BofA's base case. Brent is forecast at $91 for full-year 2026 and $80 for 2027.
A ceasefire could push it toward $80 or lower. A continued 'neither war nor peace' state could hold it near $100.
Renewed US-Iran conflict with lower inventories and limited demand elasticity could require much higher prices to clear the market.
BofA expects a swing to a 1.5mn b/d surplus by 4Q27.
Diesel stays bullish through 2026 or until Hormuz flows normalize.
Down only 0.1% from the start of the year despite the energy shock.
Activity is expanding despite the supply shock.

risk_factors: Renewed US-Iran kinetic conflict with lower inventories, less price-responsive US shale and limited short-run demand elasticity could push Brent toward $150/bbl in 2027.
Depleted Chinese and OECD strategic stocks leave less protection against another supply shock.
A pickup in shipping incidents in October threatens the recovery in Hormuz crude flows.
Product supply stays tight from Middle East and Russian refinery outages.
A 'neither war nor peace' status quo could keep the physical market tight and Brent near triple digits.
vol_and_positioning: The front-over-third-month Brent premium reached $21/bbl at its peak, a very rare level of backwardation.
Dated Brent has traded at a steep premium to front-month contracts, and BofA calls the prompt physical market acutely scarce.
Long-dated Brent and WTI have barely moved during the conflict, a sharp divergence from prompt prices.
Kalshi prediction markets put little probability on a US-Iran nuclear deal in the short term and more on a deal within 12-24 months.
geopolitical: The US-Iran war is central to the oil price path over the next 12 months, and BofA asks whether Democratic midterm gains set the stage for a peace deal.
Hormuz disruption: the IEA estimated more than 10mn b/d of Gulf production was shut in during August, and shipping incidents picked up in October.
Saudi-Houthi conflict and the Northern Red Sea route, with Saudi Arabia rerouting nearly 4mn b/d through the East-West pipeline.
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries have cut Russian refinery utilization and product exports.
A ceasefire in the US-Iran, Saudi-Houthi or Russia-Ukraine conflicts could unlock constrained production and normalize trade routes.

tension_points.bull_case: A 'neither war nor peace' status quo keeps the physical market structurally tight and could hold Brent near triple digits. Renewed US-Iran conflict could push Brent toward $150/bbl in 2027 given lower inventories and limited demand elasticity.
tension_points.bear_case: A ceasefire in the US-Iran, Saudi-Houthi or Russia-Ukraine conflicts could unlock production and return the market to surplus, pushing Brent toward $80 or lower. Long-dated prices already discount normalization.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A ceasefire in the US-Iran, Saudi-Houthi or Russia-Ukraine conflicts that normalizes trade routes and refinery utilization would invalidate the tight-market thesis.

theme_stances.key_argument: The market absorbed the shock using inventories, but the cushion is being depleted, leaving less protection against another shock.
theme_stances.evidence: substantially less protection against the next one

theme_stances.key_argument: Refinery outages in Russia and the Middle East keep product markets tighter than crude, and diesel stays bullish through 2026.
